title: Annotation, documentation, POS tagging, and ambiguity
summary: Give the six annotation levels with an example each; recite the data-linguist process and why datasheets matter; distinguish parsing from POS tagging; name the three kinds of ambiguity with examples; compare Brown and Penn Treebank tagsets; explain why no tagger reaches 100%.
sourceNote: Lecture 7 (Sep 15) and Lecture 8 (Sep 17) slides, Gebru et al. 2018, Leech 2004 ch. 2, J&M ch. 18, HW 2.

blocks.label: why
blocks.md: **The idea** A raw corpus is a pile of strings. Ask it 'how often is *book* a verb?' and it can't answer — it doesn't know what a verb is. **Annotation** adds a layer of linguistic interpretation on top of the text (this token is a verb; these four tokens are a noun phrase; this pronoun refers to that name) so that ==questions about structure become countable==. It's the difference between preprocessing — technical access to the text — and analysis.
blocks.slide: Raw text can't answer linguistic questions

blocks.body: others can check and repeat your analysis.
a computer can search 'all verbs' only if verbs are marked.
annotation guides a human reader through the data.
one annotated corpus serves many later questions.

blocks.md: **Where you'll meet this after the exam** Annotation is the 'labeled' in *labeled data* — the supervised half of machine learning trains on somebody's annotations. Content moderation runs on annotation guidelines and lives with inter-annotator disagreement; the human-feedback ratings behind chat assistants are annotation at industrial scale; and data labeling is a billion-dollar industry (Scale AI, Appen, and armies of contractors). ##The person who writes the labeling guidelines — deciding what counts as 'toxic' or 'a verb' — is doing this lecture's work for a salary, and the ambiguity section below is why the job is hard.##

blocks.caption: One pair of sentences wearing five of the six annotation layers (phonetic needs audio). Bottom to top: a morphological gloss, POS-tag chips, the tokens, a named-entity span, and a phrase-structure bracketing — plus a discourse link reaching in from the next sentence. Each layer is somebody's labeling decisions, which is why each has its own guidelines and its own disagreements. Hover any layer.

blocks.md: The morphological and syntactic rows are LING 112's interlinear glosses and phrase-structure trees, stored as data. A treebank is a corpus where every sentence has the tree you'd draw in syntax class. That's why the Penn Treebank tagset is 'theoretically committed to constituency grammar' — its designers had a syntax theory in mind.

**Where you'll meet this after the exam** The six levels are a product map. Lexical: grammar checkers and predictive keyboards. Phonetic: every voice assistant's recognizer is trained on TIMIT-style time-aligned speech. Semantic: the 'add flight to calendar' chip popping up in your email is named-entity annotation cashed in, and search knows Istanbul is a city for the same reason. Discourse: a summarizer is useless until it can resolve who 'she' is. ==A job posting that says 'NLP pipeline' means software that adds these layers, in roughly this order.==

sections.heading: The data-linguist process and why documentation matters

blocks.body: 'this is where many linguistic decisions happen.'
(tokenization, normalization — last chapter).
then iterate.

blocks.md: The full loop, in order: **1. research question and hypotheses → 2. data design decisions → 3. data collection and shaping → 4. data documentation → 5. analysis and evaluation** — then iterate. The cards above flesh out steps 2, 3, and 5; step 1 is where the 'design the dataset around the question' thesis lives, and ==step 4 is the step everyone skips and later regrets== — it gets its own block below.

**The shift she keeps naming** Traditional corpus work: *'here is a dataset — what can I do with it?'* Contemporary work: *'what dataset do I need, and how do I design it?'* The linguist as **data architect**. Her Lecture 7 line: =='Data cleaning and shaping is actually linguistic theory in disguise.'==

blocks.label: why
blocks.md: **Why document** A datasheet is a standard description of a dataset: who made it, why, from what, how it was cleaned, what it should and shouldn't be used for. Two framings: it's **ethical accounting** (biases and provenance on the record) and it's a **QA document** (the dataset becomes inspectable, testable, reusable). Without one, a dataset has no lineage, no known biases, no clear use case, no interpretive constraints. That last sentence is the answer to 'give one reason documenting datasets is important.'

**Where you'll meet this after the exam** Datasheets escaped the seminar room: HuggingFace expects a dataset card on every upload, Google popularized model cards for the same reason, and the EU AI Act turns data documentation into a legal requirement for high-risk systems. The five-step loop is the shape of every data-science project you'll ever run, and interviewers probe for exactly the shift Kraus names — ##candidates who ask 'what dataset does this question need?' read as senior; candidates who grab whatever CSV exists read as junior##.

blocks.prompt: Chance quiz: T/F — removing emojis can remove pragmatic information. And: one reason documenting your dataset matters.
blocks.answer: True (🙄 marks sarcasm). Documentation gives the dataset a lineage and known biases, so a later user knows what it can and can't support — without it, results are uninterpretable and irreproducible.

blocks.body: analyzing a string of words to determine its grammatical structure with respect to a formal grammar. Input: tokens. Output: a parse tree.

assigning a grammatical category to each word — a *component* of parsing. A tagged corpus tells you *book* is a noun; a parsed corpus tells you whether that noun is subject, object, or inside a prepositional phrase.
rewrite rules like NP → NP RelP, VP → VP NP, VP → VP PP. The slide-9 snippet generates both readings of the Canadian-audience headline.

blocks.title: Tagging the same word two ways

frames.caption: POS tagging assigns a grammatical category to every token. Start with *Book*. Out of context it could be a noun (a book) or a verb (to book). Which is it here?

frames.note: sentence-initial, followed by an object → verb
frames.caption: It starts the sentence and is followed by *me a flight* — an imperative with objects. Verb, base form: **VB**. A tagger decides this from context, not from the word alone.

frames.note: PRP pronoun · DT determiner · NN noun
frames.caption: *me* is a personal pronoun (PRP), *a* a determiner (DT), *flight* a singular noun (NN). These are Penn Treebank tags — the standard set.

*the book*: after a determiner, it's a noun, **NN**. And *read* — past or present? Spelled the same. The tagger guessed VBD (past) here, but nothing in the sentence proves it. That's **ambiguity**, and it doesn't go away when you tokenize.

blocks.title: Two parses, and why a machine can't pick
blocks.body:
Explain the ambiguity.

1. Reading 1: [help [dog-bite victim]] — police help a person who was bitten by a dog. *bite* is a noun inside a compound.
2. Reading 2: [help dog] [bite victim] — police help a dog to bite someone. *bite* is a verb.
3. The POS tag of *bite* depends on the parse, and the parse depends on the tags — circular. What breaks the tie is world knowledge (police don't usually help dogs bite people), which a tagger doesn't have.
4. That's the chance-quiz answer for 'say something about ambiguity and language data': ambiguity doesn't disappear when you tokenize; context is needed to resolve it, and context can mislead.
blocks.slide: Why 'Police help dog bite victim' is hard

blocks.md: **Where you'll meet this after the exam** POS tagging runs inside tools you touched today. Grammar checkers flag 'their going to lose' by tagging — a possessive directly before a verb is the tell; voice assistants tag 'Book me a flight' to hear the imperative verb before they search a single fare; search engines separate the brand *Windows* from *windows* partly on tags and casing; predictive keyboards weight the next word by its category. And every 'crash blossom' headline that fools a news aggregator — *Police help dog bite victim* — is ==this section's circularity problem, live in production==.

blocks.body: (for the 1961 Brown Corpus): motivated by distributional linguistics, not committed to a syntactic theory; relatively coarse on verbs. NN, NNS, VB, VBD, JJ, RB.
(early 1990s): mapped from Brown but expanded with finer, theory-committed distinctions — the most widely used tagset in NLP. Where Brown has 2 verb categories for base/past, PTB has 6.

blocks.term: PTB puts tense in the tag, not the tree
blocks.body: VBD (past: *she walked*) vs VBN (past participle: *she has walked*). Particle vs preposition: RP (*looked up the answer*) vs IN (*looked up the stairs*).
more tags = more expressive, harder to annotate consistently.

**Chance quiz: T/F — the Brown tagset has more tags than the Penn Treebank** Argue from granularity, not raw counts. PTB *expands* Brown's distinctions (2 verb tags → 6) and is the finer, theory-committed set — so the intended answer is false. (Raw tag counts are murky — Brown's full list runs to ~80+ with compound tags, PTB's core is 45 — which is exactly why she wants the granularity argument.)
hand-written disambiguation rules. Fast, transparent, brittle.
HMMs, maximum entropy — trained on annotated corpora. ('But how were *those* annotated?' — the chicken-and-egg she draws on the slide.)
transformers with wide context. Best accuracy, least interpretable.

blocks.md: All three families top out short of perfect: !!no tagger reaches 100%!!, and the errors are not random — they cluster on syntactically complex or rare constructions and at sentence boundaries, which is often exactly where the linguistically interesting data lives.

blocks.title: Every line marked DECISION is a place to write a sentence in your discussion about what it did to the data.
blocks.body:
import nltk
from nltk.corpus import brown
from collections import Counter
nltk.download('brown'); nltk.download('universal_tagset')

words  = brown.words(categories='news')                 # tokens, NLTK's tokenization (DECISION)
tagged = brown.tagged_words(categories='news', tagset='universal')

freq   = Counter(w.lower() for w in words)              # lowercasing (DECISION: Apple/apple merge)
freq.most_common(20)
types, tokens = len(set(words)), len(words)
ttr = types / tokens                                    # only comparable across same-size categories

tag_freq = Counter(t for _, t in tagged)                # POS distribution
nouns    = Counter(w.lower() for w, t in tagged if t == 'NOUN')

import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame(freq.most_common(), columns=['word', 'count'])
df['per_million'] = df['count'] / tokens * 1_000_000    # relative frequency

**Where HW 1's lost points live** In every homework discussion, write one paragraph on *what my preprocessing decisions did*: lowercasing merged *Apple/apple*; NLTK split *don't* into *do* + *n't*; TTR across categories of different sizes isn't comparable; the tagger's errors cluster at sentence boundaries. That paragraph is what she grades for.

blocks.md: **Where you'll meet this after the exam** `import spacy` puts a neural tagger one line away in any Python job, and this section's trade-off — finer categories vs consistent labeling — reappears every time a team designs a tagging scheme for support tickets, products, or content moderation. The chicken-and-egg on the slide ('trained on corpora annotated by earlier taggers') is today's synthetic-data debate in miniature. And knowing that ==errors cluster exactly where the data gets interesting== is the habit called error analysis — the single most hireable reflex in applied ML.

**Lectures 7–8 in one paragraph.** Annotation adds linguistic interpretation at six levels (lexical, phonetic, morphological, syntactic, semantic, discourse). The data-linguist process is question → design → shape → document → analyze; datasheets give a dataset lineage and limits. POS tagging assigns a category per token and is one part of parsing; ambiguity is lexical, syntactic, or pragmatic and needs context (sometimes world knowledge) to resolve. Penn Treebank refines Brown's tags; rule-based, statistical, and neural taggers all fall short of 100%.

exercises.title: Tag it, then say where a tagger would fail
exercises.prompt: Give Penn Treebank tags for every word in: 'Flying planes can be dangerous.' Give both readings. Then name the one word whose tag decides the reading, and say what a statistical tagger would probably do and why.
hints: Reading 1: planes that are flying are dangerous (Flying is an adjective-like modifier of planes). Reading 2: the act of flying planes is dangerous (Flying is a gerund verb taking 'planes' as its object).
The typical answer stops at 'it's ambiguous'. The question asks for two complete tag sequences and for *which tag* differs — that's the precision Kraus grades for.

PTB: VBG for the -ing verb form (used for both gerunds and participles); JJ for an adjective. 'planes' is NNS either way; 'can' MD; 'be' VB; 'dangerous' JJ. A tagger sees 'Flying' sentence-initially before a plural noun and picks by frequency in its training data.
solution: Reading 1 (planes that fly): Flying/VBG (participle modifying planes) planes/NNS can/MD be/VB dangerous/JJ ./. — some annotators would use JJ for 'Flying' here.
Reading 2 (the activity): Flying/VBG (gerund, head of the subject) planes/NNS can/MD be/VB dangerous/JJ ./.

The deciding word is 'Flying' — VBG-as-modifier (or JJ) versus VBG-as-gerund-head. PTB's tag alone doesn't distinguish them; the *tree* does (is 'planes' the head of the subject or the object of 'Flying'?).

A statistical tagger will output VBG for 'Flying' either way, because sentence-initial -ing words before nouns are overwhelmingly VBG in the Wall Street Journal. It won't 'see' the ambiguity — which is Kraus's point: tagging doesn't resolve ambiguity; it papers over it.
exercises.why: This is Chomsky's example, and it's on every NLP course because it shows the limit of tagging: the tag can be 'right' while the meaning is still open. Knowing where a pipeline hides ambiguity is what makes you able to audit one.

exercises.title: Write the datasheet questions you'd ask
exercises.prompt: Someone hands you 'a corpus of 50,000 tweets about the election' with no documentation. List six questions a datasheet should answer for it, grouped as: how it was collected, how it was cleaned, what it can and can't be used for. For two of them, say what goes wrong if the answer is bad.
hints: Gebru et al.'s sections: motivation, composition, collection process, preprocessing/cleaning, uses, distribution, maintenance. Pick questions from collection, cleaning, and uses.

The thin answer lists generic questions ('what's in it?'). Make each one specific to tweets: which keywords or hashtags selected them? which language filter? were retweets kept? were emojis or URLs stripped?
For 'what goes wrong': if the tweets were selected by one hashtag, you've sampled one side's vocabulary; if retweets were kept, a single viral tweet may be 5% of your tokens.
solution: Collection: (1) What query — keywords, hashtags, accounts — selected these tweets, and on what dates? (2) Was there a language or location filter, and how was it applied?
Cleaning: (3) Were retweets and duplicates removed? (4) Were URLs, @mentions, emojis, or hashtags stripped or kept, and were tweets lowercased?

Uses: (5) What research question was it built for, and what populations does it not represent (people without Twitter accounts; suspended accounts)? (6) Can it be redistributed given Twitter's terms, and are user IDs anonymized?

If (1) is one partisan hashtag, any 'both sides' analysis is invalid — you sampled one community. If (3) kept retweets, frequency counts are dominated by a few viral texts and your TTR and keyword lists describe those, not the discourse.
exercises.why: Every model trained on undocumented data inherits its blind spots invisibly; datasheets are the industry's answer, and writing one is now a routine part of shipping a dataset. Being the person who asks these six questions before the analysis starts is the job Kraus is training you for.
